Floating-point addition is not associative because modern computers represent real numbers with finite precision. In exact arithmetic, changing the grouping of a sum does not change its value: adding a and b first, then c, is equivalent to adding b and c first, then a. In floating-point arithmetic, however, the exact result of each operation is usually rounded to the nearest representable number. Different groupings create different intermediate results, so rounding occurs at different points and can produce different final answers.

The effect is especially visible when numbers have very different magnitudes or when positive and negative terms nearly cancel. If a very small number is added to a much larger number, the small contribution may fall below the available precision and disappear during rounding. If several small numbers are added together first, their combined value may become large enough to affect the later addition. Thus, even when every individual operation follows the IEEE 754 standard correctly, the order of operations can alter the result. Fused multiply-add instructions, which compute a multiplication and addition with only one final rounding, can also produce results that differ from separate multiply and add instructions, while still being more accurate in many cases.

Large matrix multiplications contain many such reductions. Each output element is a dot product, formed by multiplying corresponding entries from a row and a column and summing all the products. A sequential implementation might accumulate those products from left to right. A parallel CPU implementation may divide them among threads, compute partial sums, and combine those sums in a tree. A GPU may use a different tree based on thread blocks, warp scheduling, vector widths, or specialized matrix hardware. Distributed execution introduces another level of partial sums across devices or machines.

Because these reduction orders generate different intermediate values, they produce slightly different rounding errors. The discrepancies are normally small, but they can grow with long reductions, poorly scaled data, severe cancellation, or repeated numerical computations. As a result, two mathematically equivalent matrix multiplications can fail to be bit-for-bit identical across thread counts, hardware generations, libraries, compiler settings, or runs whose scheduling is nondeterministic.

Reproducibility therefore requires more than using the same input data and nominal algorithm. It may require a fixed reduction tree, deterministic library modes, consistent precision and fused-operation settings, or specialized summation methods such as pairwise, compensated, or higher-precision accumulation. These measures can reduce variability or improve accuracy, but they may cost performance and do not automatically make results identical across all architectures. In practice, numerical software often tests matrix results with tolerances rather than exact equality, while applications requiring strict reproducibility must explicitly control how reductions are performed.
